title: No. 12 — The Utility of the Union In Respect to Revenue (Hamilton)
paragraphs: The effects of Union on the commercial prosperity of the States have been sufficiently set out. Its tendency to promote the interests of revenue will be the subject of our present inquiry.

The prosperity of commerce is now seen and acknowledged by all enlightened statesmen to be the most useful, and the most productive, source of national wealth, and has accordingly become a primary object of their political concern. By multiplying the means of gratification, by promoting the introduction and circulation of the precious metals—those darling objects of human avarice and enterprise—it serves to enliven and invigorate the channels of industry and to make them flow with greater activity and abundance. The diligent merchant, the laborious farmer, the active mechanic, and the industrious manufacturer—all classes of men—look forward with eager expectation and growing eagerness to this pleasing reward of their toil. The often-debated question between agriculture and commerce has, from undeniable experience, received a verdict that has silenced the rivalry once between them and has proved, to the satisfaction of their friends, that their interests are intimately blended and interwoven. It has been found in various countries that as commerce flourishes, land rises in value. And how could it have been otherwise? Could that which provides a freer outlet for the products of the earth, which furnishes new incentives to cultivate land, which is the most powerful instrument for increasing the quantity of money in a state—could that, in short, which is the faithful handmaid of labor and industry in every form, fail to enlarge that very thing which is the prolific parent of by far the greatest part of the objects on which they are exerted? It is astonishing that so simple a truth should ever have had an opponent. It is one among many proofs of how easily a spirit of ill-informed jealousy, or of too great abstraction and refinement, can lead men astray from the plainest truths of reason and conviction.

The ability of a country to pay taxes must always be largely proportioned to the quantity of money in circulation, and to the speed at which it circulates. Commerce, contributing to both, must necessarily make the payment of taxes easier and ease the supply of funds to the treasury. The hereditary dominions of the Emperor of Germany contain a great extent of fertile, cultivated, and populous territory, much of it located in mild and luxuriant climates. In some parts are to be found the best gold and silver mines in Europe. And yet, lacking the fostering influence of commerce, that monarch can boast only slender revenues. He has several times had to depend on the financial support of other nations to preserve his essential interests, and he is unable, on the strength of his own resources, to sustain a long or continued war.

But it is not only in this respect that the Union will be seen to serve the purposes of revenue. There are other points of view in which its influence will appear more immediate and decisive. It is plain from the state of the country, from the habits of the people, and from our own experience on the matter, that it is impractical to raise any very considerable sums by direct taxation. Tax laws have been multiplied in vain; new methods of enforcing collection have been tried in vain; the public expectation has been uniformly disappointed, and the treasuries of the States have remained empty. The popular system of administration inherent in popular government, combined with the real scarcity of money that comes with a languid and crippled state of trade, has so far defeated every attempt at extensive collections, and has at length taught the various legislatures the folly of trying.

No one familiar with what happens in other countries will be surprised at this. In so wealthy a nation as Britain, where direct taxes from greater wealth must be much more bearable, and from the vigor of the government much more practicable, than in America, by far the largest part of the national revenue is derived from indirect taxes—from imposts and excises. Duties on imported articles form a large branch of this latter category.

In America, it is plain that we must depend for a long time mainly on such duties for revenue. In most parts of the country, excises must be confined within a narrow range. The temper of the people will not bear the inquisitive and peremptory spirit of excise laws. The pockets of the farmers, on the other hand, will reluctantly yield only scanty supplies in the unwelcome form of taxes on their houses and lands; and personal property is too uncertain and invisible a fund to be reached in any way other than by the imperceptible operation of taxes on consumption.

If these remarks have any foundation, then the state of things that will best enable us to develop and extend so valuable a resource must be best suited to our political welfare. And it cannot be seriously doubted that this state of things must rest on the basis of a general Union. So far as the Union would advance the interests of commerce, it must extend the revenue drawn from that source. So far as it would help make regulations for the collection of duties simpler and more effective, it must serve to make the same rate of duties more productive, and to put it in the power of the government to raise the rate without harm to trade.

The relative position of these States; the number of rivers running through them and bays washing their shores; the ease of communication in every direction; the affinity of language and manners; the familiar habits of intercourse—all these are circumstances that would together make illicit trade between them a matter of little difficulty and would ensure frequent evasions of one another's commercial regulations. The separate States or confederacies would be forced by mutual jealousy to avoid the temptations to that kind of trade by keeping their duties low. The temper of our governments, for a long time to come, would not permit those rigorous precautions by which the European nations guard the entrances to their countries, by land as well as by water—and which, even there, prove insufficient obstacles to the adventurous stratagems of avarice.

In France, there is an army of patrols (as they are called) constantly employed to secure their fiscal regulations against the inroads of dealers in contraband trade. Mr. Necker estimates the number of these patrols at over twenty thousand. This shows the immense difficulty of preventing that kind of traffic where there is inland communication, and casts a strong light on the disadvantages that would burden the collection of duties in this country if disunion placed the States in a situation, relative to each other, resembling that of France relative to her neighbors. The arbitrary and vexatious powers with which the patrols are necessarily armed would be intolerable in a free country.

If, on the contrary, there is but one government extending over all the States, then for the principal part of our commerce there will be only ONE SIDE to guard—the ATLANTIC COAST. Vessels arriving directly from foreign countries, laden with valuable cargoes, would rarely choose to risk themselves to the complicated and critical dangers of unloading before reaching port. They would have to fear both the dangers of the coast and of detection, both after and before their arrival at their final destination. An ordinary degree of vigilance would be enough to prevent any major infringements on the rights of the revenue. A few armed vessels, judiciously stationed at the entrances of our ports, might at small expense be made useful sentinels of the laws. And since the government would have the same interest in guarding against violations everywhere, the cooperation of its measures in each State would tend powerfully to make them effective. Here too, by Union, we would preserve an advantage nature holds out to us and which would be given up by separation. The United States lie at a great distance from Europe and at a considerable distance from all other places with which they would have extensive trade connections. The passage from them to us in a few hours or in a single night, as between the coasts of France and Britain and other neighboring nations, would be impossible. This is a prodigious security against direct contraband with foreign countries. But a roundabout contraband into one State through another State would be both easy and safe. The difference between direct importation from abroad and indirect importation through a neighboring State, in small parcels, according to time and opportunity, with the additional facilities of inland communication, must be obvious to every discerning man.

It is therefore plain that one national government would be able, at far less expense, to extend the duties on imports beyond comparison further than would be practical for the States separately, or for any partial confederacies. Up to now, I believe it can safely be said that these duties have not on average exceeded three percent in any State. In France they are estimated at about fifteen percent, and in Britain they exceed this rate.(1) There seems to be nothing to prevent their being raised in this country to at least triple their present amount. The single article of ardent spirits, under federal regulation, could be made to yield a considerable revenue. Based on the import figures for this State, the whole quantity imported into the United States may be estimated at four million gallons—which, at a shilling per gallon, would produce two hundred thousand pounds. That article would easily bear this rate of duty; and if it tended to reduce consumption, such an effect would be equally favorable to the agriculture, the economy, the morals, and the health of society. There is perhaps nothing so much a subject of national extravagance as these spirits.

What will be the consequence if we cannot make use of this resource to its full extent? A nation cannot long exist without revenues. Without this essential support, it must surrender its independence and sink into the degraded condition of a province. This is an extremity to which no government will willingly agree. Revenue, therefore, must be obtained at all costs. In this country, if the main part is not drawn from commerce, it must fall with oppressive weight on land. It has already been suggested that excises, in their proper sense, are too little in tune with the feelings of the people to allow great use of that mode of taxation. Nor indeed, in States where agriculture is almost the sole employment, are the objects proper for excise numerous enough to allow very large collections that way. Personal property (as already noted) cannot, owing to the difficulty of tracing it, be subjected to large contributions by any means other than taxes on consumption. In populous cities, it may be enough the subject of conjecture to occasion oppression of individuals without much aggregate benefit to the State; but beyond those circles it must largely escape the eye and the hand of the tax-gatherer. Since the necessities of the State must nevertheless be satisfied in one way or another, the lack of other resources must throw the principal weight of public burdens onto the owners of land. And on the other hand, since the wants of the government can never be adequately supplied unless all sources of revenue are open to its demands, the finances of the community, under such embarrassments, cannot be put into a state consistent with its respectability or its security. So we will not even have the consolation of a full treasury to make up for the oppression of that valuable class of citizens employed in the cultivation of the soil. Public and private distress will keep pace with each other in gloomy concert, and will join in lamenting the infatuation of those counsels that led to disunion.
1. If my memory is right they amount to twenty percent.
